label: TypeScript
description: Type-system MCQ: inference, unions and narrowing, generics, utility types, strict mode and conditional types.

questions.title: Which statement about `interface` and `type` is correct?
questions.prompt: Which statement about `interface` and `type` is correct?

options.text: Only `interface` supports declaration merging; a second `type` alias with the same name is a duplicate identifier
Only `type` supports declaration merging; a second `interface` with the same name is an error
Both merge automatically, in declaration order
Neither can be extended or combined

questions.explanation: Interfaces are open: declaring `interface User` twice merges the members. A type alias is a closed declaration, so a second `type User` is a duplicate identifier. Unions, tuples and primitives require `type` anyway.

questions.title: What does the compiler report for this code?
questions.prompt: What does the compiler report for this code?

options.text: Nothing — `count` becomes `any` and accepts the string
Error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'
Error TS2339: Property 'three' does not exist

questions.explanation: `let count = 0` infers the widened type `number`, so assigning a string is a type error. `const` would infer the literal type `0` instead.

questions.title: A function receives JSON from the network. Why is `unknown` preferred over `any`?
questions.prompt: A function receives JSON from the network. Why is `unknown` preferred over `any`?

options.text: `unknown` is faster at runtime because it skips type erasure
`unknown` accepts every value, but reading a property on it is a compile error until the type is narrowed
`any` cannot be used when `strict` is enabled
`unknown` can only hold primitives, never objects

questions.explanation: Both accept any value, but `any` switches type checking off for that value. `unknown` is the safe top type: narrow it with `typeof`, `in` or a type guard before use.

questions.title: Given `interface User { id: string; name: string }`, which type makes both properties optional?
questions.prompt: Given `interface User { id: string; name: string }`, which type makes both properties optional?
questions.explanation: `Partial<T>` maps every property to `T[K] | undefined`. `Required<T>` is the inverse, `Readonly<T>` blocks reassignment and `Record<K, V>` builds an object type from a key set.

questions.title: A generic helper must accept anything with a length. Which change makes this compile?
questions.prompt: A generic helper must accept anything with a length. Which change makes this compile?

options.text: `function longest<T extends { length: number }>(a: T, b: T)`
`function longest(a: any, b: any)` is the only fix

questions.explanation: An unconstrained `T` could be `number`, which has no `length`, so TS reports "Property 'length' does not exist on type 'T'". A constraint documents the requirement and keeps the return type generic.

questions.title: Which property access is safe inside these branches?
questions.prompt: Which property access is safe inside these branches?

options.text: Both are errors unless the properties are optional
Both are safe: the `kind` discriminant narrows the union in each branch
Only the first branch is safe; the second needs a cast
Neither is safe — a discriminated union must be checked with `in`

questions.explanation: A shared literal field (`kind`) is a discriminant. Comparing it narrows the union, so `radius` is valid in the `circle` branch and `side` in the remaining `square` branch.

questions.title: What is the inferred type of `config`, and what happens on the last line?
questions.prompt: What is the inferred type of `config`, and what happens on the last line?

options.text: No error — `as const` only affects string values
`as const` makes the object deeply readonly with literal types (`"dark"`, `3`), so the assignment is a compile error
The assignment throws a TypeError at runtime

questions.explanation: `as const` produces a readonly object whose properties are literal types — useful for config objects and for deriving unions such as `typeof config.mode`.

questions.title: `strict: true` is enabled. What does the compiler require here?
questions.prompt: `strict: true` is enabled. What does the compiler require here?

options.text: The `undefined` case must be handled before calling `.slice`, because `strictNullChecks` makes `name` of type `string | undefined`
The parameter must get a default value; narrowing is never enough

questions.explanation: Under `strictNullChecks`, an optional parameter is `string | undefined`, so it must be narrowed (`if (!name) return ""`, `name ?? ""`, or a justified `name!`) before member access.

questions.title: Which annotation types this callback without implicit `any`?
questions.prompt: Which annotation types this callback without implicit `any`?
questions.explanation: A function type declares parameter and return types and gives the parameters contextual types, so they are not implicit `any`. `Function` is effectively untyped and `void` discards the returned number.

questions.title: What is the return type of this accessor, and why does it compile?
questions.prompt: What is the return type of this accessor, and why does it compile?

options.text: `T[K]` — the indexed access type follows the requested key, and `K extends keyof T` keeps it within the object
`keyof T` — the key union is returned
`T` — generics always return the generic parameter

questions.explanation: `T[K]` is a lookup type: it resolves to the property type of the key actually passed. Constraining `K` with `keyof T` rejects unknown keys, so no cast is needed inside.

questions.title: What is the type of `Available`, and how does `Exclude` produce it?
questions.prompt: What is the type of `Available`, and how does `Exclude` produce it?

options.text: `"draft" | "active"` — `Exclude` is `T extends U ? never : T`, so matching members are filtered out

questions.explanation: `Exclude<T, U>` is a conditional type that distributes over the union: members assignable to `U` become `never` and drop out, leaving `"draft" | "active"`.

questions.title: Why does the second assignment fail while the first is fine?
questions.prompt: Why does the second assignment fail while the first is fine?

options.text: Fresh object literals get excess property checks, so unknown keys are rejected; assigning a pre-existing variable only needs structural compatibility
`const` objects are readonly and can never be assigned to an interface
Interfaces are nominally typed and require a `class` implementation
The error is about the missing `balance` declaration, not the literal

questions.explanation: TypeScript is structural: `ACCOUNT` is assignable because it has `id`. Excess property checking is an extra guard applied to fresh literal expressions, which is why the inline literal with `balance` is rejected unless widened through a variable or assertion.

questions.title: Which can declare an array or function type?
questions.prompt: Which can declare an array or function type?

options.text: Both type and interface can describe object shapes, arrays and function types

questions.explanation: Both work: `type Fn = () => void` as well as `interface Fn { (): void }`. They mainly differ in declaration merging and extends syntax.

questions.title: What happens to `(v) => v` under strict mode when v has no annotation?
questions.prompt: What happens to `(v) => v` under strict mode when v has no annotation?

options.text: A compile error — implicit any is disallowed

questions.explanation: noImplicitAny (enabled by strict) flags untyped parameters instead of silently widening them to `any`.

questions.title: What does `function echo<T>(v: T): T` guarantee?
questions.prompt: What does `function echo<T>(v: T): T` guarantee?

options.text: The returned type matches the argument type for each call

questions.explanation: The type parameter links input to output: echo(5) infers T = number, so the result is typed number.

questions.title: What does strictNullChecks change for `string | null`?
questions.prompt: What does strictNullChecks change for `string | null`?

options.text: null is a distinct type — accessing members without narrowing is an error

questions.explanation: You must guard (null checks, optional chaining) before treating the value as a string.

questions.title: What does `Partial<T>` produce?
questions.prompt: What does `Partial<T>` produce?
questions.explanation: Partial maps every key to optional — ideal for PATCH payloads where any subset of fields may be present.

questions.title: How does `typeof x === "string"` narrow `x: string | number`?
questions.prompt: How does `typeof x === "string"` narrow `x: string | number`?

options.text: The true-branch treats x as string automatically

questions.explanation: typeof is a built-in type guard; no assertion is required inside the guarded branch.

questions.title: What does `() => void` mean as a parameter type?
questions.prompt: What does `() => void` mean as a parameter type?

options.text: The function must return void exactly
Any function callable with no arguments whose result is ignored

questions.explanation: A void-returning function type accepts functions that do return something — the caller simply ignores the value.

questions.title: What is a string literal type?
questions.prompt: What is a string literal type?

options.text: A type restricted to one exact string such as "on" | "off"

questions.explanation: Literal types pin exact values, giving autocomplete and exhaustiveness checks for small unions.

questions.title: Does TypeScript use nominal or structural typing?
questions.prompt: Does TypeScript use nominal or structural typing?
questions.explanation: Compatibility depends on members, not declared identity — two unrelated types with matching members are interchangeable.

questions.title: What does `as const` do?
questions.prompt: What does `as const` do?

options.text: Bakes in literal types and readonly-ness instead of widening
Marks the value immutable at runtime

questions.explanation: Without it `["a","b"]` widens to string[]; with it the literal stays readonly ["a", "b"].

questions.title: What is the difference between `Omit<T, K>` and `Pick<T, K>`?
questions.prompt: What is the difference between `Omit<T, K>` and `Pick<T, K>`?

options.text: Pick keeps only the listed keys; Omit keeps everything except them

questions.explanation: `Pick<T, "a">` selects "a", while `Omit<T, "a">` is `Pick<T, Exclude<keyof T, "a">>` — the same machinery, opposite direction.

questions.title: Why is `typeof x === "object"` an imperfect narrowing check?
questions.prompt: Why is `typeof x === "object"` an imperfect narrowing check?

options.text: typeof null is "object" and arrays are objects too, so both survive
It is not allowed in TS

questions.explanation: Add `x !== null` and `Array.isArray(x)` to separate those cases — otherwise the union still contains them.

questions.title: What does `keyof T` produce?
questions.prompt: What does `keyof T` produce?

options.text: A union of T's property names

questions.explanation: `keyof T` is a union of keys, enabling `T[K]`, `Record<keyof T, ...>` and `<K extends keyof T>` constraints.

questions.title: What does `T extends U ? X : Y` do inside a generic type?
questions.prompt: What does `T extends U ? X : Y` do inside a generic type?

options.text: It resolves once T is instantiated, choosing X or Y based on the actual argument
Creates a union of T and U

questions.explanation: Conditional types defer resolution until the type argument is known — the foundation of utility types like Exclude and NonNullable.

questions.title: What does `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` change?
questions.prompt: What does `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` change?

options.text: Indexed access now includes | undefined, forcing a missing-key check

questions.explanation: Object/array indexes aren't guaranteed to exist at runtime; the flag surfaces that reality in the types.

questions.title: When is `x as T` appropriate?
questions.prompt: When is `x as T` appropriate?

options.text: When you can guarantee the fact the compiler cannot — e.g. after your own validation of a union

questions.explanation: Assertions that state something verifiable are fine; using them to bypass real type errors just hides bugs.

questions.title: When is `interface` the better choice?
questions.prompt: When is `interface` the better choice?

options.text: When you want declaration merging or cleaner messages for object shapes

questions.explanation: Interfaces merge across declarations (useful for extending library types); type is required for unions, tuples and mapped types.

questions.title: Is a required parameter allowed after an optional one?
questions.prompt: Is a required parameter allowed after an optional one?

options.text: No — TypeScript rejects a required parameter following an optional one

questions.explanation: The call signature would be ambiguous, so TS errors; reorder the parameters or make the later one optional.

questions.title: What does `T["name"]` mean?
questions.prompt: What does `T["name"]` mean?
questions.explanation: Indexed access types extract a member's type from a type — the building block for derived utility types.

questions.title: Why do fresh object literals with extra keys error if typing is structural?
questions.prompt: Why do fresh object literals with extra keys error if typing is structural?

options.text: Excess property checking applies only to fresh literals, catching typos before they ship

questions.explanation: Assigning a broader variable is allowed, but a literal with unknown properties is a classic typo risk, so TS flags it.

questions.title: What is the difference between `<T extends object>` and `<T>` with no constraint?
questions.prompt: What is the difference between `<T extends object>` and `<T>` with no constraint?

options.text: The constraint lets you safely index T and warns callers before instantiation rather than erroring inside the body
Only the first supports default parameters

questions.explanation: Deferring the check to the call site gives callers a precise error and keeps generic bodies usable — the constraint moves from body to boundary.

questions.title: Why do you need `infer` in a conditional type?
questions.prompt: Why do you need `infer` in a conditional type?

options.text: To capture a matched sub-type as a new type parameter inside the true branch

questions.explanation: `T extends Promise<infer V> ? V : never` captures the inner type — the basis of ReturnType, Awaited and similar helpers.

questions.title: How does `Record<Union, T>` differ from indexing a mapped type with optional keys?
questions.prompt: How does `Record<Union, T>` differ from indexing a mapped type with optional keys?

options.text: Record guarantees every union member is a required key — making it ideal for exhaustive maps with lookup by literal
Record only works with string unions

questions.explanation: Combined with a switch or a lookup table it prevents silently missing cases: the type demands an entry for each member.

questions.title: What does `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` change?
questions.prompt: What does `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` change?

options.text: It separates 'absent' from 'present but undefined' — `{ a: undefined }` no longer satisfies `a?: string`

questions.explanation: By default undefined is assignable to optional keys; the flag makes absence explicit, which matters for APIs distinguishing null vs missing.

questions.title: What does a discriminated union rely on?
questions.prompt: What does a discriminated union rely on?

options.text: A common literal field (like `type: "loading"`) shared across members

questions.explanation: Switching on the discriminant narrows the whole union — the standard pattern for state machines and event reducers.

questions.title: What does `interface User extends Required<Partial<User>>`-style self-extension risk?
questions.prompt: What does `interface User extends Required<Partial<User>>`-style self-extension risk?

options.text: Circular or infinitely recursive type expansion can error during declaration merging

questions.explanation: Interfaces are resolved eagerly when merged/extended; self-referential constructions can exceed the compiler's depth limits.

questions.title: What is `satisfies` useful for that `as` is not?
questions.prompt: What is `satisfies` useful for that `as` is not?

options.text: It checks the expression against a type without widening its inferred literal/shape, preserving precise types

questions.explanation: `const routes = {...} satisfies RouteConfig` validates the object yet keeps its exact literal keys for later narrowing — `as` would erase that precision.

questions.title: What does `T extends Record<keyof T, unknown>` achieve as a constraint?
questions.prompt: What does `T extends Record<keyof T, unknown>` achieve as a constraint?

options.text: It forces T to be a map
It requires T to declare all of its own keys — a self-referential shape check without needing an interface

questions.explanation: The constraint pins T to its own key set (a 'no extra keys' check) while still letting callers pass any compatible literal.

questions.title: Why can a callback with fewer parameters be passed where more are expected?
questions.prompt: Why can a callback with fewer parameters be passed where more are expected?

options.text: Parameter bivariance lets a function ignore extra arguments — providing fewer is safe

questions.explanation: A function of arity 1 can legally stand in for an arity-3 callback because JS ignores extra arguments; TS mirrors that.

questions.title: Why are `type User = { name: string }` and a class with the same members interchangeable, and how do you opt out?
questions.prompt: Why are `type User = { name: string }` and a class with the same members interchangeable, and how do you opt out?

options.text: Structural typing allows it; nominal intent requires a private brand field or unique symbol

questions.explanation: TS is structural, so to prevent accidental compatibility you add a private property (only the declaring class can make one) or a unique symbol brand.
